chapters.title: Chapter 3: Valuing a Business Against Its Peers

lessons.title: Valuation Multiples Explained: P/E, EV/EBITDA and EV/Revenue

children.text: Somebody in your next meeting will say a business is worth "20 times earnings" or "8 times EBITDA" and everyone will nod. A multiple is the fastest way to price a business and the easiest way to be wrong, because the whole argument is hidden inside one number. This lesson takes that number apart.

body.text: A multiple is not a valuation method. It is a summary of one, borrowed from other companies. When you say a business is worth 20 times earnings, you are saying it deserves the same growth and the same risk as whoever else trades at 20 times.

children.text: What a Multiple Actually Is
Every multiple is a price divided by something the business produces. Change the thing in the denominator and you change who the multiple is measuring for.

body.caption: The three multiples you will meet most often

cells: Equity holders only, after interest and tax
The whole business, before debt and tax
The whole business, when there is no profit to divide by

children.text: The first uses
equity value
, the other two use
enterprise value
. Mixing them up is the single most common error in Indian deal conversations.

markDefs.definition: What the shareholders own: the market capitalisation of a listed company, or the price paid for 100% of the shares of a private one.
The value of the whole operating business, funded by both shareholders and lenders. Broadly equity value plus debt, less cash. Lesson 3.2 builds this bridge properly.

children.text: Worked Example: Deccan Foods
Deccan Foods Limited is a fictional listed packaged foods company. Its shares trade at ₹150 and it has 10 crore shares outstanding.

stats.label: Net debt
stats.context: ₹300 crore of debt less ₹100 crore of cash

body.caption: All three multiples for the same company

body.text: Flip the P/E over and it becomes an earnings yield: 1 ÷ 30 = 3.3%. That is what the business earns each year for every rupee of share price. Set that against a 10 year G-sec at about 7% and you can see immediately that buyers of this stock are paying for growth, not for current earnings. Every high multiple is a bet on the future.

body.title: Compute the enterprise multiple
body.prompt: A company has a market capitalisation of ₹1,700 crore, debt of ₹500 crore, cash of ₹200 crore and EBITDA of ₹250 crore. What is its EV/EBITDA multiple? Give the answer as a number of times.
body.explanation: Enterprise value = ₹1,700 crore + ₹500 crore - ₹200 crore = ₹2,000 crore. ₹2,000 crore ÷ ₹250 crore = 8 times. Note that cash is subtracted: a buyer effectively gets that cash back on day one, so it reduces the real cost of the business.

children.text: Trailing or Forward, and Why the Gap Matters

A multiple needs a period attached to it. Trailing multiples use the last reported 12 months. Forward multiples use next year's expected figure. For a growing company the two can look completely different.

body.caption: Deccan Foods, same share price of ₹150

body.text: A seller will quote the forward multiple because it looks cheaper. A buyer will quote the trailing one because it is verified. Neither is dishonest, but comparing a trailing multiple for one company with a forward multiple for another is meaningless. Always ask which year the denominator comes from.

children.text: Why Deals Prefer EV/EBITDA
P/E is fine for comparing listed shares. It falls apart the moment two companies carry different debt, because interest sits above the earnings line while debt itself sits outside the P/E entirely.

body.title: Two identical cement plants, different balance sheets

columns.label: Company A: no debt
points: Higher profit after tax, so a lower P/E at the same price
Looks "cheaper" on P/E purely because of the balance sheet
Buyer acquires a business with nothing to repay

columns.label: Company B: ₹600 crore of debt
points: Same EBITDA ₹100 crore, but interest crushes the bottom line
Lower profit after tax, so a higher P/E at the same price
Looks "expensive" on P/E while the plants run identically
Buyer must also take on or repay ₹600 crore

children.text: EV/EBITDA fixes this. It compares the value of the whole business against the profit the whole business generates, before financing. That is why almost every mid-market deal in India is quoted as a multiple of EBITDA.

body.title: From a peer multiple to a price for the shares
body.prompt: Comparable listed companies trade at an EV/EBITDA of 10 times. Your target has EBITDA of ₹60 crore, debt of ₹200 crore and cash of ₹50 crore. What is the implied value of its equity, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Enterprise value = 10 × ₹60 crore = ₹600 crore. Net debt = ₹200 crore - ₹50 crore = ₹150 crore. Equity value = ₹600 crore - ₹150 crore = ₹450 crore. The multiple gives you the value of the business, not the cheque the shareholders receive. Lesson 3.2 is entirely about this step.

children.text: When There Are No Profits: EV/Revenue
Early-stage and fast-growing businesses often have no profit to multiply, so buyers fall back on revenue. It is a blunt instrument, because it says nothing about whether those sales make money.

body.label: Hindustan Unilever's purchase of Minimalist
body.context: The January 2025 deal valued the skincare brand at ₹2,955 crore against FY24 revenue of ₹347 crore. That multiple reflected a specific brand with specific margins bought by a specific acquirer. It does not make every Indian D2C brand worth 8.5 times revenue, though you will hear founders quote it as though it does.

body.text: A revenue multiple silently assumes a margin. If two brands both do ₹100 crore of revenue and one earns 20% EBITDA while the other earns 5%, the same revenue multiple values them identically. That is not a valuation, it is a coin toss.

children.text: The Multiples Indian Sectors Actually Use

cells: Debt is raw material for a lender, so enterprise value has no meaning. Book value proxies the capital at work
EV/EBITDA, and enterprise value per tonne of capacity
Capacity is comparable across companies. Industry rules of thumb put the cost of building new capacity at roughly $120 to $140 a tonne, which anchors what buying existing capacity should cost
EV/EBITDA, and enterprise value per room
Rooms are the unit of capacity, and location drives the value per room enormously
Asset light, low debt and predictable margins
Stable earnings and brand value that assets do not capture
Net asset value of the project pipeline and land bank
Value sits in individual projects, not in a single year's profit
Profits emerge over decades, so a single year's earnings tells you little

body.text: Notice the pattern. Where capacity is physical and comparable, the market invents a per-unit multiple: per tonne, per room, per subscriber. Where profits arrive over decades, it uses a value measure instead of an earnings measure. The sector convention exists because the general purpose multiple failed there first.

children.text: Where Is the Market Trading?
Any multiple needs a reference point. The index P/E is the crudest one available and still the most quoted.

body.label: Nifty 50 price to earnings ratio
body.context: As at 15 September 2026, against a five year median of roughly 22. When someone claims a business deserves 40 times earnings, that is the number to hold it against, and the burden is on them to explain what makes the business worth double the index.

body.title: Why a multiple is a discounted cash flow in disguise

children.text: For a business growing at a constant rate, value equals next year's cash flow divided by the discount rate less the growth rate. Divide both sides by earnings and you get the multiple.

content.caption: The same value driver formula from Lesson 2.2, expressed per rupee of earnings

children.text: Read what that means in practice. A higher P/E is justified by faster growth, by higher returns on capital, or by lower risk. Nothing else. If a company claims a premium multiple, ask which of those three it has, and what evidence supports the claim.
Higher growth, same risk: a higher multiple is justified
Higher returns on capital, same growth: a higher multiple is justified, because less profit must be reinvested
Higher risk, same growth: a lower multiple is justified, no matter how exciting the story
Six Ways a Multiple Misleads

body.caption: Traps to check for before you quote a multiple

cells: Comparing this year's number with next year's
Which financial year is the denominator?
A land sale or an insurance claim inflates earnings, so the multiple looks low
Is this normalised earnings or reported earnings?
Under Ind AS 116, rent moves into depreciation and interest, lifting EBITDA for retailers and airlines
Are both companies on the same lease treatment?
Applying a fast grower's multiple to a slow grower
Does this business have the same growth and risk as the peers?
One extreme peer drags the average away from reality
What does the median peer trade at, and what is the range?
Using an old balance sheet to convert enterprise value into equity value
As at what date are the debt and cash figures?

body.title: Which multiple would you use?
body.question: You are comparing two logistics companies with identical operations. One has borrowed heavily to buy its fleet, the other leases and carries no debt. Which multiple gives the fairer comparison of the businesses themselves?
options: P/E, because it captures the bottom line
EV/EBITDA, because it values the whole business before financing costs
EV/Revenue, because revenue is unaffected by accounting
Price to book, because both own fleets
body.explanation: Interest on the borrowings depresses the leveraged company's earnings and inflates its P/E even though the trucks run the same way. EV/EBITDA compares business against business. Watch the lease treatment though: if one company's leases sit in EBITDA as rent and the other's do not, adjust before comparing.

body.title: "Brands like ours sell at 8 times revenue"
body.scenario: You are the CFO of a ₹120 crore revenue D2C personal care brand. The founder circulates a note to the board claiming the company is worth ₹960 crore, because "HUL bought Minimalist at 8 times revenue". Your brand earns a 6% EBITDA margin. Minimalist was widely reported to be profitable with far stronger gross margins, and was bought by a strategic acquirer with a nationwide distribution network.
body.prompt: How do you respond to the board without simply dismissing the number?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Agree on what the comparable actually was. One transaction, in January 2025, for a specific brand, bought by a specific acquirer that could plug it into its own distribution. That is a participant specific price, not a market rate.
2. Compare the economics, not just the revenue. At a 6% EBITDA margin we generate about ₹7.2 crore of EBITDA on ₹120 crore of revenue. At 8 times revenue we would be asking ₹960 crore, which is over 130 times EBITDA. Stating it that way makes the ask visible.
3. Build the valuation from at least two angles: an EV/EBITDA range from comparable transactions, and a revenue multiple range across several deals rather than the single most flattering one.
4. Identify what would justify a higher multiple: gross margin, repeat purchase rate, customer acquisition cost, growth rate and channel mix. These are the things a strategic buyer pays for, and they are improvable.
5. Ask who the likely buyer is. A financial investor will pay for cash flows. A strategic acquirer may pay for distribution fit. The plausible buyer set determines the plausible multiple.
6. Present a range with the assumptions written down, not a single headline number. A board that anchors on ₹960 crore will treat every real offer as an insult.

body.title: Turn it upside down
body.textWithBlank: The reciprocal of the P/E ratio is the earnings ___, which lets you compare a share directly against a bond yield.
body.explanation: A P/E of 25 is an earnings yield of 4%. Holding that against the 10 year G-sec yield is a quick reality check on how much growth the price is assuming.

body.title: Before you quote any multiple
steps: State whether it is an equity multiple or an enterprise multiple, and use the matching numerator
Name the financial year of the denominator, and say whether it is trailing or forward
Confirm the denominator is normalised, with one-off items removed
Check that the peers share the business model, growth rate and risk profile, not just the industry name
Use the median of the peer set, and disclose the range around it
Take net debt from the most recent balance sheet date, and note that date
Sanity check the result against the index multiple and against a second method

body.label: Screener.in: screens by P/E and EV/EBITDA
body.description: Build a peer set for any Indian listed company and compare P/E, EV/EBITDA, growth and return on capital side by side. Notice how often the cheapest multiple in a sector belongs to the company with the weakest growth.

cards.definition: Share price divided by earnings per share. An equity multiple, sensitive to debt and tax.
The reciprocal of P/E, comparable with a bond yield.
Equity value plus debt less cash. The value of the whole operating business.
The workhorse deal multiple, comparable across different capital structures.
Used when there are no profits. Silently assumes a margin.
Based on the last reported 12 months of actual results.
Based on the next year's expected figure, and only as good as the forecast.
Market value of equity divided by book value. The convention for banks and lenders.

points: A multiple is a borrowed valuation. It imports somebody else's growth, returns and risk into your company.
P/E measures value to shareholders. EV/EBITDA and EV/Revenue measure the whole business, which is why deals use them.
For Deccan Foods, ₹150 a share meant a P/E of 30, an EV of ₹1,700 crore and an EV/EBITDA of about 14.2 times, all from the same set of facts.
A peer multiple gives you enterprise value. Subtract net debt to reach what shareholders actually receive.
Revenue multiples assume a margin. Restate any revenue multiple as an EBITDA multiple before believing it.
Sectors invent their own units, such as enterprise value per tonne of cement capacity or per hotel room, when the general purpose multiple fails.
The Nifty 50 traded at about 19.5 times earnings in mid-September 2026. Any premium to that has to be earned by growth, returns or lower risk.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Deccan Foods and the D2C brand in the scenario are fictional. The Nifty 50 P/E and sector rules of thumb quoted are as at September 2026, change constantly, and differ between data providers depending on whether standalone or consolidated earnings are used.
